title: Earth's highest clouds form about 80 km up, where the air is colder than −120 °C
body: Noctilucent clouds float **76 to 85 km** above the ground, far above any weather, near the top of the mesosphere, the coldest part of Earth's atmosphere. They are made of tiny ice crystals up to 100 nanometres across, which only form below about −120 °C and are thought to grow on dust left by burning micrometeors. They appear in summer at latitudes of about 50° to 70°, and they are so faint that you can only see them in twilight, glowing in sunlight after the Sun has set for the ground below. That is where the name comes from: it means night-shining.

cover.alt: Dark globe seen from above the North Pole, with faint wisps of blue-white cloud scattered over the Arctic around a black circle at the pole

slides.alt: Dark globe seen from above the Arctic. Faint blue-white wisps of cloud appear over the polar region and thicken day by day into a bright, patchy ring around a black disc at the North Pole.
slides.caption: NASA's AIM satellite maps the 2007 noctilucent cloud season over the Arctic, 31 May to 1 July, about 1.5 days a second. Blue-white patches are the clouds; the black disc is a gap in coverage.
slides.credit: NASA Scientific Visualization Studio · Public domain · excerpt

slides.heading: How high noctilucent clouds float
slides.note: The clouds sit between about 76 and 85 km

slides.heading: Meteors, and maybe methane
slides.text: The dust at the heart of each crystal is thought to be meteoric smoke. Some of the water may come from methane reacting high in the atmosphere, so more methane in the air could mean more water vapour, and more of these clouds.

events.text: AIM, the first satellite built to study them, launches on 25 April

slides.question: When can you see noctilucent clouds from the ground?
slides.explanation: They are too faint to see by day. They show up best when the Sun is between 6° and 16° below the horizon: dark for you, but still sunlit 80 km up.
